chunks.text: U-substitution is the chain rule run backward, used to integrate composite functions.
An integrand suited to u-substitution has a composed function multiplied by the derivative of its inner function, like 2x·cos(x²).
The five steps are: choose u as the inner function, compute du and solve for dx, rewrite the integral in u, integrate, then substitute back or change limits.
Choose u as the inner function of a composition, such as u = 3x + 1 in ∫cos(3x + 1) dx.
Choose u as the part whose derivative also appears, such as u = x³ in ∫x²·e^(x³) dx since x² is a constant multiple of the derivative of x³.
When integrating a power of a complicated base, let u be the base, such as u = 2x + 5 in ∫(2x + 5)⁷ dx.
If du does not appear in the integrand even after adjusting for a constant, the choice of u is wrong and a different u should be tried.
Example: ∫2x·cos(x²) dx with u = x², du = 2x dx becomes ∫cos u du = sin(x²) + C.
Example: ∫(3x + 1)⁵ dx with u = 3x + 1, du = 3 dx, dx = du/3 gives (3x + 1)⁶/18 + C.
Example: ∫x·√(x² + 9) dx with u = x² + 9, x dx = du/2 gives (1/3)(x² + 9)^(3/2) + C.
Example: ∫tan x dx = ∫sin x/cos x dx with u = cos x, du = −sin x dx gives −ln|cos x| + C.
You may adjust for a constant factor, such as writing x dx = du/2, because constants pull outside the integral.
You cannot pull a function of x outside the integral; if x-terms remain after substituting, the substitution has not worked.
If leftover x's remain, either rewrite them in terms of u using the substitution equation (e.g., u = x² + 1 gives x² = u − 1) or choose a different u.
For definite integrals, one option is to keep the original x-limits and substitute back to x before evaluating.
The cleaner option for definite integrals is to change the limits to u-values: x = a becomes u = g(a) and x = b becomes u = g(b).
When the limits are changed to u-values, you must not substitute back to x; mixing the two methods gives a wrong answer.
Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of x·(x² + 1)³ dx with u = x² + 1 changes the limits to u = 1 and u = 5, giving the value 78.
Always match the variable of the antiderivative to the variable of the limits: evaluate a u-expression at u-limits, never at x-limits.
Stating the new limits explicitly, such as 'when x = 2, u = 5,' makes the work clear and earns method points.
An indefinite-integral result from u-substitution can be verified by differentiating to recover the original integrand.
U-substitution is the most important integration technique in AP Calculus AB and recurs in accumulation, area, and volume problems.
